newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Rights issues said blocking new EU-ASEAN pact.
newsitem.headline: Rights issues said blocking new EU-ASEAN pact.

text.p: European and Southeast Asian nations were set on Thursday to agree on a plan to broaden ties, despite differences over human rights issues such as East Timor and Burma, delegates said.

The 15-nation European Union (EU) and the seven members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) would adopt an action plan to boost political, economic, cultural and security ties, they said.
But Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said EU member Portugal was still blocking a new treaty between ASEAN and the EU that would formalise taking relations to a new level.
"(East Timor) was one of the issues used by Portugal to prevent a new-generation agreement to be signed by the two sides, and of course we deeply regret it," Alatas told reporters.
"Right now, we are cooperating on the basis of the old agreement with some modifications," he said.
Last June, an Emminent Persons Group laid out dozens of proposals for a new agreement aimed at bringing the two regions closer.
A senior ASEAN official said a new pact would have the status of a treaty and thus needed the consent of all signatories, something Portugal has so far refused to give.

But a draft declaration to be approved by foreign ministers on Friday adopts a number of projects -- from educational exchanges to cooperating on terrorism and crime as well as new trade initiatives -- that would go into a treaty, he said.
"We can still have the substance, even without the form," the ASEAN official said.
The old pact, signed in 1980 when the relationship was largely defined by European aid to former colonies in Asia, needed to be updated or replaced, he said.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. All but Thailand are former European colonies.
Delegates said the EU was also reluctant to extend any pact to Burma, which is due to join ASEAN, possibly as early as this year, along with Laos and Cambodia.
Much of the preparatory talk has centred on Burma. Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar told reporters that the ministers had spent most of a two-hour lunch talking about it.
"This was one of the most productive and substantive discussions between the EU and ASEAN held to date," he said.
Jayakumar gave no details of the talks but suggested the gap between the two attitudes to Burma's military government had not changed.

"Not that each side has convinced the other. But both sides agreed that we now have, as a result of the dialogue, a better understanding of each other's insights, concerns and approaches on Myanmar (Burma)," he said.

The EU believes tough measures are needed to punish the Rangoon government for its crackdown on Burma's pro-democracy movement, while ASEAN believes "constructive engagement" will eventually coax the military regime into reforms.
Delegates said Burma might be mentioned in the final declaration, but East Timor would not. Indonesia had threatened to walk out of the conference if it appeared in the declaration.
But a Portuguese diplomat told Reuters the EU officials had agreed to raise the East Timor issue during the discussions.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 after a civil war followed Portugal's abrupt decolonisation of the territory. Up to a third of the population died in the famine and fighting that followed.
Indonesia then annexed East Timor in 1976, but the United Nations still considers Portugal the administering power.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said in an interview with Reuters Television that Burma and East Timor would not be "a hindrance" at the meeting.
"I don't think they are going to be a hindrance. I think formulae have been found to deal with them."
